accounts.title: Developer accounts
does: Accounts GitHub places in Algeria at the end of the quarter
A running total since accounts were created
doesnt: Active developers: dormant accounts still count
People using a VPN, who appear elsewhere

pushes.title: Pushes per account
does: Pushes in the quarter, divided by all accounts
Web-interface edits, which count as pushes
doesnt: Commits: one push can hold many

repos.title: Public repositories per account
does: Public repositories per account, both running totals

orgs.title: Organisations per account
does: GitHub organisations per account: teams, companies, clubs
doesnt: Size or activity of each organisation

topics.title: Topics above GitHub’s threshold
topics.note: GitHub publishes a topic once 100+ developers use it
does: Topics GitHub publishes for Algeria: those used by 100+ developers

permillion.title: Accounts per million people
does: Developer accounts relative to population (World Bank, latest year)
doesnt: The share of people who code

trends.fig2_lede_dip: Growth slowed from {first} in {y0} to {low} in {ylow}, then jumped to {last} in {yn}, the fastest pace in the series.

trends.why_index_text: Indexing sets every economy to 100 at the start of {year}, so the lines compare growth, not size. In {last}, Algeria stands at {dz}: {times} times its level in {first}. {peer} stands at {peer_value}, the highest of the six peers.
trends.why_median: Why a median, not an average?
trends.why_median_text: Seven economies is a small group. One large value, like {country}’s {value} accounts, would pull an average up. The median is the middle value, so one outlier can’t move it far.
